utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you are to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. We're now going to carry on with your statement, as we said it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to have the help of the usher to have the document DD00-2005, please. That's page 14 of the English version, and page 15 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, after that paragraph which you read yourself yesterday, carry on down your statement, I'd like to you take a look at what comes right after paragraph (c) at the left of the screen, or rather, the paragraph at the left of the screen which starts with: "Nevertheless." In the earlier paragraph, which we already commented on, you were referring to the military situation in Sarajevo and consequences for the civilian population, right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You've used -- I'm now going to translate it into French, but you used the word "traps" for civilians. They were caught in a trap. Could you just say the word in the microphone so it's in the transcript. You used the word which is the equivalent of trap?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the burden of the bombardment fell on the civilians trapped within the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, since by your profession as a journalist, you had to travel everywhere through Bosnia. You can put it like that, right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were acquainted with the situation of civilians elsewhere, all over, in the rest Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you then say that everywhere, other than Sarajevo, civilians with the help of the Red Cross and other international organisations were helped to leave, to flee mostly to western countries.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult for them to flee, madam. Some people did manage to get out early in the war from Sarajevo. Civilians were trapped, not by the encirclement of an enclave, not only in Sarajevo but in the Lasva Valley where the Croats could not get out. So it was not a situation totally unique to the civilians in Sarajevo, but those on the government side of the lines were, of course, facing an encirclement; whereas, those on the Serbian side of the lines were able to get out to safer territory, if they wished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But would you say, and here I'm concerned with the time between August 1994 and up to the Dayton agreements, did you know of the existence of a tunnel in Dobrinja, leading to Igman and free territory basically, of government forces of Bosnian forces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. The press were, of course, kept away from it for reasons of operational security. My understanding was that its uses were mostly military and that the Bosnian government forces were able to use it to bring reinforcements into the city. But if an ordinary civilian wished to use the tunnel to get from inside out, that would have required special permissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you perhaps know about the person who was in charge of handing out these permits?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But one may say that the tunnel was not in fact used to evacuate civilians who is wanted to get out of the city itself, of the city centre of Sarajevo, that part that was held by the forces of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as I am aware, they were not able to do so on any significant scale. I didn't -- I didn't see any great difference in the population of the size of the population of Sarajevo at that stage of the war relative to what it had been three years ago, three years before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you did see that there was a difference between the military activities during the period where you were in Sarajevo. I'm speaking of the entire duration of the conflict. There were different areas, so to speak, in that conflict, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes there were. The intensity of the fighting fluctuated. There were times of relatively lull and quiet, and I would specify, for example, in January of 1995. There are times when it reached a real peak and the worst of these were the summer of 1992 and the summer of 1995, with the addition of what I said in my evidence to Ms. Edgerton, that some new weapons were also deployed and there were signs of an of an implement attempt by the Bosnian government side to break the siege in the spring/early summer of 1995. So the military -- the answer to your question is that the front lines were nearly all the same, that the military situation was not constant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, you say in your statement, and that's the last sentence basically, the last paragraph on page 14: "The Serbs were on the defensive [In English] throughout 1995." Does that confirm what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to them early in the war and I had a long session with Dr. Zametica, actually, and I said this is going to happen. A time will come when the manpower on the government side is so great and yours is so little that you will have difficulty holding your lined. And this in fact happened with an attempt to break out of the city and into it. It actually got across the Pale road, and yes, I would say that certainly from the time when Glamoc and Grahovo were lost in the previous year. I would say that the -- that the Bosnian Serbs were on the defensive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we conclude from that that on the other side government forces, the ABiH, were in fact on the offensive?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only the army of BH. They were preparing for an offensive, which they delivered and which actually didn't quite succeed. But the Croats were breaking through on the -- on the western flank, and the big change in the military situation came from the HVO and regular forces from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But at that time - I'm now referring to 1994 and 1995 - they were together, right? They were on the same side, the Croat army and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, against the forces of the Republika Srpska, right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, and that is one reason why the forces of the Republika Srpska were on the defensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But before that, since you're familiar with the situation even before 1994, did you know of anything about the relations that existed between the HVO and the army of the Republika Srpska? That's before they allied with the forces of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard reports of actually liaison between the two armies, though I never saw it for myself. This was, of course, the time of what I call the side war between the army of BiH and the Croats, chiefly in Central Bosnia, and the Serbs were stood aside from that. It was not their war, but clearly it helped them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know at the time the hospital at Blazuj, near Ilidza, it was called -- well, it wasn't actually a hospital. It was a wartime hospital. It was called Zetra in Blazuj, near Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did visit one Bosnian Serb field hospital, but it was not that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me get back to the time for which my client is accused before this Chamber, that's August 1994, coming towards the end of the war. Is it correct to say that the situation of civilians was also fluctuating as a consequence of the military activities that were going on in the theatre of operations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. When there was a lull in the fighting, it was safer for civilians to walk the streets and there was more chance that basic supplies of gas and electricity and water would also be restored. So it depended entirely on the fighting and the external access to the city and the point of relief flights coming into Sarajevo airport. And that -- what I'm saying that the plight of the civilians in Sarajevo on both sides, like the fighting itself, fluctuated and that the two bore a relation to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear anything about tunnels being used to bring food into the city; that is, that part of the city which was in the hands of the forces of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear reports of that. As I explained for reasons of operational security, we were -- the press was kept away from tunnels. But I think to be realistic, it could have been only on a reflectively small scale because of the size of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to apologise before the Chamber and my learned colleagues that I can quote neither the page nor the line of the transcript, since we were not able to use a quote last night, neither at home nor in the room of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember saying the following, I'd like you to confirm it. "The situation regarding food improved around the spring of 1995." Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably said that. This would have been the consequence of at least two months of -- of relative calm in the city; but then, of course, when the fighting started, it deteriorated again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Ms. Edgerton is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If it assists, I have the copies of the transcript of yesterday in English, the relative pages. I can refer my friend to, and I'm happy to provide those -- the copy of the transcript to Mr. Bell, if that might assist his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be helpful, but it seems as if he has agreed that he did say that. So let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, yesterday, we looked at several videos showing the plight of the civilians and filmed by you, your own cameraman, and commented by yourself sometimes. Unfortunately, there were no dates on those videos.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the transcript, I'm now going to give the names of these exhibits, which have been put in as exhibits without dates P609, P610, P613, P614, P615, P617, P618, P619.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'd now like you to confirm for me, or deny, that these videos, with no dates, were in fact filmed between August 1994 and 1995; that is, towards the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to do that without having these videos before me. I think most of them were from that period, but it is possible that some of the early sniper videos of snipers corner were taken before August 1994; on the other hand, I'm sure that the videos involving the French armoured vehicles were taken during and shown during the period relevant -- immediately relevant to this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You also said yesterday - this time I do have the page in the working version of the transcript. I noted it. It was page 68, line 28 - in which you said that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was trying to draw attention, the attention of public opinion. Do you remember saying that, and can you confirm it today?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can one say then, having looked at all these videos and you confirmed something about this yesterday, that a lot of incidents -- sniping incidents happened around the Holiday Inn, in front of the Holiday Inn Hotel. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the sniping incidents in my experience happened in that area and about four, 500 metres to the east in what became known as snipers corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And yesterday, with Ms. Edgerton, you talked about an incident in which a girl was, I believe, shot dead on August 11th, 1994. And you said - I'd like you to confirm it if you can - that this happened near headquarters, the headquarters of the ABiH, and that journalists were there and filmed it. Is this something that you can confirm?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm, and I would like to ample fly that if I may. It -- the girl was shot actually not outside the main corps headquarters but outside the press office, which was separate in a different area from the corps headquarters, and I think it was separate for reasons of operational security so that the journalists could come and go without a lot of security. It just happened to be in that street, but it was just the press office of the corps that was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, there was something that you said yesterday in your testimony, and I have tried to recollect it and my colleagues have confirmed. I believe you said that the ABiH had a political interest in provoking some of the incidents. Do you remember saying something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I said that, and I have written it on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you explain what the interest is? What do you mean by a political interest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The army of the ABiH and the government side were facing a very critical situation, especially in their relative lack of heavy weapons that they would only be able to break the siege by making sacrificial attacks, which is what they attempted. They were all the time, I think, from the beginning of the war to the end, looking for outside intervention, to help them; and to that reason, they were not going to sit quietly under a siege. They had an eloquent spokesman in Haris Silajdzic, who consistently used the media to call for outside intervention. So, yes, I think it is best to explain, if you like, there were two conflicts going on in the city. One was a conflict between two armies; the Bosnian Serb army and the ABiH. But there were also bombardments of civilian areas and the -- and the sniping at civilians, which I would say happened on both sides and were against the rules of law, as I understand them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you recall any particular incident which you might be able to say was provoked by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a -- there was fighting on the 24th of May, which started very early in the morning, and which, as I remember, led the Bosnian Serbs to take their heavy weapons back out of the special zones where they had been put in safe areas. This was part of a previous deal. And they went and seized them because they felt their lines were -- were going to be overrun so they took their heavy weapons back. And that was what led General Smith to -- to threaten the Bosnian Serbs with retaliation, which happened, and that in turn led to the seizing of UN military observers and other UN personnel by the Bosnian Serbs as hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally what form would this provocation take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ABiH had mortars. It knew where the Bosnian Serbs positions were. They would, from time to time, use their mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you mean that they would initiate an attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They certainly initiated an attack when they tried and, indeed, succeeded in crossing the Pale road, I think, early in June 1995. That was -- we actually had video of their infantry. It was on a long shot. You could see them snaking up the hill to storm the position. I mean, it was -- it was a war fought on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bell. Could I just pick up on your distinction between the two wars. Who waged the second war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, Your Honour, the second war was waged on both sides but the preponderance of it by the -- by the Bosnian Serbs. Both sides had snipers. There is evidence of civilians being targeted and, indeed, killed on both sides, but there were many fewer civilians left there Grbavica, which was the area most in danger. If you drove through Grbavica, you would see these tarpaulins, the sheets, on lines across the road, which were put there in order to -- to blind the snipers. The shocking thing, to my point of view, because I mean I understand wars between main forces. I have been there lots of them, but I had not seen the targeting of civilians. Well, I had been in Rwanda but I hadn't seen the targeting of civilians on this scale before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question really was whether the so-called the second war was fought between the military forces; that is to say, that they were fought out by personnel which formed part of the military structure, and thus under command of the responsible officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, you will find that as the war went on, the armies became increasingly structured and increasingly professional. When the war began, you would find on the Bosnian Serb side militia men and soldiers with Chetnik insignia; that is, the old irregulars going back. Those were removed from the uniforms. The Bosnian Serb army prided itself on being a correct and disciplined military force, and the ABiH was also. It got rid of some of its dissident elements. There is was a notorious character called Juka who was driven out and fled and joined the Croats in Mostar. I would have thought by the end of 1992, the armies were much more like regular armies than they were when the war began, with chain of commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just to be sure that I have understood you correctly put the same question from the back side; namely, to say that it is it your understanding that civilians did not themselves take a direct part in the conflict. They did not take to arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They obviously did in so far as they were recruited into the military; and if you were a young man of military age, you had little chose over than to serve. In the early weeks, anybody who had a gun picked it up and used it; but as the war developed, no, I would discount the idea that there was any significant freelance military activity, except for gangsterdom and criminality, which did occur, especially within the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I'm going to carry on in the same direction. I earlier asked you about this specific incident that had occurred in front of the press centre. Now, just before the anti-sniping agreement was signed, you also referred to one of your memories. I don't know exactly when the incident happened, but you did tell us there were people waiting for water. They were queueing up to get water, that you yourself were present, and that you filmed that time when those people started being shot at. You were right there. Can you confirm saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that, and I was there. But if it is any help to you, this was in a period before that -- to which this Court is investing itself. It was during the winter of 1992 to 1993 that the sniping of the water pipes -- standing pipes was particularly acute, because that was when the water shortage was the most acute.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, that is at page 61 of the transcript from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't take a note of the page number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I have now given a few examples, and I'm going to give some more of situations that had one thing in common; that is, the presence of journalists right when the incident was happening. Can you put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident -- I mean, there were many incidents happening when there were no journalists there. I would be very reluctant to suggest that anything happened because there were journalists. We're talking about a relatively small area, one end to another maybe about two miles. The press corps was never less than about 50 strong. They were around in the streets a lot. There were many water points in the winter of 1992 to 1993. There would not have been any press around at all. I happened to be doing a documentary, a longer programme, and I wanted to show something of the plight of the people. I simply wanted to show them getting their water in difficult circumstances. But while this was happening, this man was shot at. It was happening all the time and most of it frankly went unrecorded and unmarked by the press. It was part of daily life.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We have also watched videos of what happened at Markale. That's the incident of Markale 2 on August 28th, 1995. And since in this Chamber we've seen quite a few exhibits that relate to this incident, I'd like it ask you whether you think it is fair to say that journalists went there faster, in fact, than even the local police, if you look at the video?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the video, as we remember, was in two sections. One was my edited report, most of which was shot, I would have thought, 15, 20 minutes after the attack, but it was quite obvious there was one camera very close and on the scene immediately. Again, this wouldn't altogether surprise me. This was a time when the press corps was increasing in numbers because it had been a very active and dangerous summer, and I don't think that any particular significance can be read into the fact that there happened to be a camera nearby. It would is been very odd if in the middle of the morning or around market time, there hadn't been a camera around anywhere. It was a city with a lot of the cameras in it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: While on the subject of these provocations, or rather, to begin with, before anything else, it is very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have this exhibit tendered, DD00-2085, if I could have a number for that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this a document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: It's the document that's on the screen before you. It's a technical issue. Before I can move to another document, I have to have it tendered as evidence. Now, I'd like to you take a look to watch a video together. This is one of your films. On the list, it has the number 4D.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That was the video that was shot on September 4th, 1994. Do you recall these events, this video?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is, in my opinion, a good example, this particular video. Your colleague is in this studio back at the BBC and is summarizing basically what is going on. What you've shot lasts roughly two minutes, and some conclusion had to be made, have to be drawn in order to draw the interest of the viewers. That's the way it works, correct? Is that the way it works?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think in this case conclusions were necessary. Editorialising was not necessary. The difficulties of arranging the Pope's visit because of the insecurity in Sarajevo at the time would get the viewer's attention anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What I think is interesting is that your colleague back home in the BBC studies says that the Serbs can't guarantee the Pope's safety. Is that something that we with agree on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said. I am not sure I want to be held responsible for what the news reader says in the studio. I would stand by what I wrote there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not. I am merely trying to analyse how things work in the media, with your help because are you in the best position to explain it to us. Can we then agree that hearing what was being said in that news reel, the word "Serb" and that of "safety" are put together. It's the Serbs that can't guarantee the safety of the Pope?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that. We have -- we had a difficulty there. At the time, I don't think we were able to get to Pale. Those pictures would say have been sent from Pale to London, the pictures of Karadzic and slotted into the report. Now, there were times when the Serbs said, in 1995, they could not guarantee the safety of UN flights, and I would then say that that was taken by the UN to be a threat against -- against their flights. But looking at that exhibit, I think it stands up pretty well as a fair-minded report, that the Pope's safety was threatened by the war, and either side could have provoked or carried out an incident on that time and blamed it on the other. And as I also pointed out, there were others at risk besides his own. I haven't seen that since I did it, but I'm not ashamed of having done it, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I quite agree with you. But this very way of working for the television news is being discussed in the west. The idea is that it presents to us, the television viewer sitting around the dinner table, a vision of what is going on far away but which is of a concern to us, as human beings, even though we're sitting in there, eating, and looking at disasters far away. This way of doing things, would you say that it requires for one thing to draw everybody's attention, one thing to trigger the attention so that people will go on watching? Would you say that beyond this particular video that is the way that you make television news?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it is the way television news is sometimes made. It is, for instance, extremely difficult to get a television programme to accept a story about peacemaking or post-war reconstruction. But at the height of the war, we didn't need any editorialising, any tricks, any slight of hand. The images and the facts of what was happening were themselves sufficient to attract and keep the attention of the viewers. I didn't see any artifice in that particular -- I see that as a very straight report, that example you gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, to what part of your case is all of this relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I may use my own methods, so to speak, and "slight of hand," to quote, I have my own documents that I want to show Mr. Bell. We're going to look at them together and in the perspective of what the television viewer sitting back home in Britain was watching. Looking at what was going on in Sarajevo and based on the documents of UNPROFOR. This, I think, can be an interesting exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not here for interesting exercises. I'm asking how does this effect the question of the criminal liability of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, actually, Your Honour, you know that the case of the Defence is, as it has been shown several times, that the media were doing a lot of manipulation to do with the role of the army of the Republika Srpska, of which my client happened to be a commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And I think this is going to be an example of what is being reported on, in good faith, but compared with the documents actually compiled by the people who are there, and who are investigating the actual event, related to this particular visit and the visit of the Pope as planned, which in the end didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that he has been wrongly charged because of exaggerated reports by the media? I'm trying to understand how it affects the liability of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Your Honour, the Defence has contested all along and will continue to contest the factual basis of this case. All those incidents that happened, that we contest, we do not agree with the version given by the Prosecutor about these incidents. What I would like to show now is the documents available and compare them with this particular news report. This witness is in a very good position to tell us, and he does talk about the interest that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But now I'm a bit lost. I've lost the thread of what I was trying to get at, but I do hope that I'm going to pick it up very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Before I was interrupted by the Judge, I was about to -- we were watching a video shown by the BBC, and there was talk about Serbs being unable to guarantee the safety of the Pope. I'm now going to ask you a question: On that day, September 4th - that's the actual date of that report - did you hear of an incident, a sniping incident, that happened to target people in Zetra. A place where they were building this alter for the planned and subsequently failed visit of the Pope, which was what provoked the lack of safety, the insecurity that you just mentioned in your report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was such an incident, if there was such an incident, Ms. Isailovic, it which must have happened after that report was compiled or, of course, I would certainly have included it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to have a look at document DD00-2123. And to begin with, were you familiar at the time with press conferences -- the press conferences given by the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever I was in the city and not otherwise engaged, I would attend these press conferences.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And what we have here is an UNPROFOR report about the events that occurred between September 3rd and 4th, 1994. According to a general assessment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: Following general assessment, you can read the paragraph, more specifically the three first sentences of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the UNPROFOR - and this was also mentioned in the regular press conference - was suggesting, in fact, that the government side, the government forces, were provoking, that they were shooting around Zetra, which was supposed to be the place where the Pope was going to speak. I assume that you had to work very quickly; and because of that, you had to leave out this UNPROFOR report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I was reporting on the day for the day. I was in the area of Zetra myself on the day. That report would have been used at the end of the day. You will see from the UN report there was no sniping activity reported in the city on that day. So whatever the relative significance of what happened the day before, I clearly considered at the time that it was not significant enough to nut my report. I'm not saying I was right. We all make mistakes, but the -- when you saw the French senior officer looking around and the preparations being made, I mean, those people would not have been making those preparations if there been serious sniping activity in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But these sniper events were going on on that very same day on September the 4th. We're now going to look at another document. It's in English. We do have a document in French, but that has already been tendered. So I'd rather show you -- I'd like you to take a look at this report of an investigation of the UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: By the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are, in fact, sniping incidents in Zetra. And these investigations tend to show that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to blame and that these sniping incidents are to be considered as a provocation. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I also see that this was included in the press briefing for the 5th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Isailovic, when you show us a document on the screen, it would be best to give us its number. I take notes myself, and I don't actually know what to call this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-2078. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, please forgive me. DD00-2116. Your Honour, I would like to have this document tendered since we can use it to demonstrate that these events were in fact known. But since we already have this document up, this is Exhibit D51. It's a report of this incompetence but it's the French version, and this is a report on the investigations carry you had by the UNPROFOR in the wake of this sniping incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I'm not quite sure of the dates. Could you help us out here. I see on the top of the screen a date which appears to be the 6th of September; and then in point 1A, it says that the HQ Sector Sarajevo sitrep, dated 04/22/00, which as we have been taught would signify the 4th of September at 10.00 p.m., states that a Danish team, and so on, had been shot at. So that would indicate that this incident did occur, in fact, on the 4th of September, and yet the report somewhere else also appears as having been made on the basis of incoming reports made on the 5th of September. So what is the exact relevant date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are many dates and that's normal in a way, because it's an investigation report from the site -- on-site report. So this is the 4th of September, 1994 -- one of the reports is on the 4th of September, 1994 and after that investigation took place; and then we have Exhibit D51 that with be shown as well. But that is already tendered into evidence. So the French team made or carried out a complete investigation on this; and following these investigations, which were carried out on the 5th of September, they drafted this report on the 6th of September. So all this looks very logical to me. It's logical that there are many dates. And if we look at the report, the report that I was showing a little bit earlier, the first report relates to the first day of the incident. So I wanted to show the witness a report that was seen by viewers in England on that day, and I wanted to put a few questions to our witness regarding that. But, first, I would like to ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document ID number DD00-2116 becomes D179.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And to be able to look at all the elements before I put the question to you, we have this document. It's D51. We see it. We see this document on the screen. I'm sorry. So we see the first page, and it's in French. Therefore, I'm going to read it for the interpreter. "Incident occurred on the 4th of September 1994 in Zetra. And in Sarajevo on the 5th of September, the following day, the investigation was carried out given the importance of what happened and following the interpretation given by the reporters of the event." Mr. Bell, I'm very glad are you here and I can ask you this question, but are reporters required to be so fast? And because of this, does that stop you from checking the information afterwards and to correct the information received eventually if something was erroneous and to say it to the viewers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, obviously, in the nature of news, we are not shooting a documentary. You gather what information you can when you can. And you prepare it as accurately and as fairly as you can. And in this particular case -- I mean, not everything that happened. There were attacks on the UN regularly all over the city at its outposts, and we didn't know about them all at the time. And, clearly, if we had been in Zetra at these hours, we would have reflected what had happened. But if you also look at your paperwork, you will see it didn't get into the UN system until late that day after I had filed my report. I mean, I cannot conceive of having known of an attack alleged by the UN to have come from the BiH forces on an UN patrol near the stadium, almost on the eve of the Pope's visit. I would have been extraordinarily negligent not to have used it in my report. I can only add that I have a reputation. My colleagues in the press corps tended to regard me as rather an odd character, that I would tend to bend over backwards to be -- to be fair to the people who were not represented on that side of the line, even though we had no direct access ourselves to Pale. In fact, I will admit that some of my colleagues thought of me as being rather pro-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But my following question is to ask you to either confirm or deny whether the role of reporters is not to carry out investigation but, rather, to show the truth. It is to inform the viewers of all the information that you have at your disposal before you show your televised report.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is always what we tried to do. To be honest, the easiest thing to report is a fire fight, a battle. One side doing this and the other side doing that. To be fair to the viewers, we tried to give it a little bit of context. Why is that side doing that? With what weapons? In what circumstances? Where can we find out how did this begin? Therefore, an element of investigation is necessary to the craft. But it's all very fragmentary because we only have a few hours to put it together. I would especially on the really difficult issues, like the reporting of atrocities, I would never go with allegations. You had to be absolutely sure before you reported something.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I forgot to ask that the video clip be tendered into file. So it was the portion that we were able to see, and then later on we can see with the Registry how we can do this. But it's the document that's bears the number 7160, from 47 minutes 51 seconds up until the end of that video clip. I was told yesterday -- the Prosecutor, rather, told me yesterday that it is important to withdraw that particular part, or to select that particular portion and to give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit that particular portion of the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you also mentioned, yesterday, that there were attacks that were carried out against the television building. We called this building the TV building. Do you recall stating that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did, and it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you've also stated that this building was always a target, was a permanent target is in a way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think permanent is right because it suggests that there are constant attacks, but there were many attacks on it over the first three and a half years. I remember standing outside it in April 1992, and we just saw one shell after another coming in on the face, roughly every two minutes. It was -- at the time, it was targeted. It was targeted by the air bomb in 1995, and there were attacks in between. But constant, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would have liked to show you a document that's part of documents that were introduced by the Defence, D103. This document relates to that shell or air bomb that hit the television building on the 28th of June, 1995. I would like to ask you to look at it briefly, and then I will ask you a question about it. This is a report stemming from the UNPROFOR, or rather, excuse me. It's an UN report. We see here that it says, "heard and saw."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we scroll down it a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. So it was by chance that this report was found. It is a report from the UNMOs, and they were stationed in Sarajevo. They describe in this report, this water collection point and they say that the shell or the projectile came from the territory controlled by the army of the -- the ABiH army. Are you surprised by this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you show me where it says that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: "Heard and saw." It's approximately where the cursor is.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I've got it. I'm not your best witness on this, Ms. Isailovic, because my colleague, Jeremy Bowen, was doing the reporting from Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, my question was to ask you whether you are now surprised by this. There is some evidence to tell us that the television building was targeted by the ABiH forces. Are you surprised by this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am surprised because I have no knowledge that they had such a weapon in their arsenal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, as a reporter and an independent reporter, you were not able to know the entire arsenal of the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would over three and more years have a pretty good idea, and nothing of this kind had been used before. I mean, I would be interested to see what the UNPROFOR briefing said about this attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this the first time you're hearing of this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not the first time that I'm hearing of the incident, but it is the first time that I'm seeing this particular UNMO's report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you said that at the time for the first time those weapons were seen, air bombs, it was the first time during that period when those bombs were seen, and that's when you heard of this new weapon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was in Sarajevo at that time, and the first use of this weapon was in Hrasnica, as we described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're not a weapons expert, I imagine?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in heavy weapons, madam, but I have been a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I am also not a weapons expert. But regarding that weapon, since the weapon in question appeared for the first time in the spring of 1995, it was considered to be a new weapon, and you did not have time to check if both sides had that weapon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my general experience of the war even then that if an army had a weapon, it would use it. They were improvising. The Croats were at one point were rolling sea mines down the hills into villages. If they had a weapon, they would use it. I would be really interested. Because you do surprise me with this document, I would be interested to see what UNPROFOR's conclusion was. We have here one report by an UNMO. I would like to see how that was presented at the following briefing. That would be helpful. But, of course, I wasn't there at the time so, as I explained, I'm not your best witness here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I wanted to show you this report because you have excluded the possibility, yesterday, of an eventual fire that could have come from the ABiH forces on two parts of the territory that they themselves held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton would like so say that that is not a correct characterisation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Ms. Edgerton would actually like to say, Your Honours, that these questions have been asked an answered and asked an answered. I think the witness has reaffirmed his answer several times that he wasn't there at the time. Mr. Bowen is the appropriate witness to comment in more detail about this. He has asked for UNPROFOR's final conclusion. The matter has been fully dealt with now several times over now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the last utterance from Ms. Isailovic was more in the form of a statement than a question. She says she wanted to show the report because, yesterday, the witness excluded the possibility of an eventual fire that could have come from the ABiH forces on two parts of the territory that they themselves held. What is you're answer to that, if indeed it was a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even if it wasn't a question, I will attempt an answer. This is the first evidence I have seen from within the UN system of any account of an attack of certainly of a heavy weapon of this kind being used by the ABiH. I don't know if this report is correct or not. I mean, if I were doing anything in this court other than being a witness, I would like to see what the -- what the UN's final conclusions were when they had done the crater analysis and everything else that they do. So I would just -- never having seen this before, if I'm allowed to, just to suspend judgement on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Isailovic, I have to conclude that you have exhausted this topic. Please move on to another area of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But before I go on to another topic, I would like to put the following question to Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this on the same topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I'm not talking about the television building anymore. It's a general question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard evidence before this Trial Chamber, and I will quote the page; page 975, line 20 of the transcript. We've heard a general, his name is Nicolai. General Nicolai was at the time the head of -- I'm not really certain what his function was at the time, but it was at the time while General Rupert Smith was the commander of the BH sector. He was working him, and he testified before this Tribunal and told us that his predecessor at the UN, a General Van Baal, talked to him and told him after the investigation that he carried out that there was at least one occasion an example when BH forces fired on the territory that they held, actually. So, Mr. Bell, General Van Baal, does that ring a bell, that name? Did you know him maybe at the time when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, that's -- I have here page 975, line 20 in front of me, and that is not what General Nicolai said. General Nicolai said, "General Van Baal, who was actually my predecessor's predecessor, told me before my departure that in one specific case, they had a very strong impression that the Bosnian Muslim forces had fired on their own people with the intention of shifting the blame towards the Bosnian Serbs," and he continued. I'm formulating it because it was very strongly his impression that that is the way it happened. They never had 100 per cent evidence of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Now Ms. Isailovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. But, in fact, I raise for this moment. In fact, I wanted to give the exact reference. I wanted to do it before but I was interrupted. The page is 1045. And during the redirect the Prosecutor, Mr. Docherty, asked a question to that effect. He wanted to know if those were rumours. But General Nicolai said that General Van Baal carried out these investigations, and that it was following those investigations that he himself was able to make this conclusion. That was on page 1045, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is not the page you quoted Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I quoted the first page that my friend was referring to, and I quoted it verbatim, Your Honours. Now I would like it if we could go to page 1045 and report exactly what General Nicolai said. He replied: "But to answer the question, was General Van Baal basing this material" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. "But to answer the question, was General Van Baal basing this upon material he had received from somebody else?" The answer was: "The answer was based on the outcome of investigations into the incident that happened during the period that he was Chief of Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is exactly what I said, Mr. President. I said the same thing, didn't I? Following the investigation, he was able to get to conclusion as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question that you wish to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already put the question to the witness before I was interrupted by my learned friend, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, did you know General Van Baal at the time of your stay?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew General Nicolai who was, as I remember, the Chief of Staff to General Smith, but I do not remember having met General Van Baal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I imagine that you never heard of this incident that General Van Baal investigated following which the conclusions were that the ABiH forces fired on their own territory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My response to that was that this would be such an important allegation and an important investigation that there must be somewhere within the paperwork of UNPROFOR a result of an investigation, rather than just a report of what one general said to another general afterwards. These are very serious matters and these allegations were raised from time to time, and we constantly tried to get to the bottom of them. I mentioned General MacKenzie having made allegations of this sort against one side or another - he didn't specify - in July 1992. I'm not a lawyer, but I would think you -- this is so serious a matter that you would expect a hard documentary evidence of the investigation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, too. They must exist and I will try and find them, but first I wanted to know if you heard of General Van Baal?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I may have heard of him; but if I did, I have forgotten. General Nicolai I did know. I think probably General Van Baal's period of office coincided with the time when I was reporting the war in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Isailovic, we're five minutes to the break, and I'm told that you have remaining about six or seven minutes for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, already now I can tell you that I would need a little bit more time. Maybe just a few more minutes, because I would like to finish my second topic that I would like to start, which was already -- which already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will grant you an extension, so let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, Exhibit 621 was tendered into evidence. It's a video from the 7th of April, 1994 relating to Hrasnica. It's a video clip, and I would have liked to see the entire clip that was shown on the BBC television the evening of the 7th of April. And I would like to ask my assistant to show us the same video clip, DD00-7160. It is a 65 ter document. It's at 30 minutes and 44 seconds. This is where it starts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we saw part of this video. Do you remember that, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, simply to have the information whole, I thought it was a good idea to watch the whole thing that was seen by the television viewers, those people who were watching the BBC that evening. And there was a part not shown by the Prosecution, and that is the part where you were standing with the soldiers of the ABiH, I believe, at a time when they were preparing for this offensive. Is that basically right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You have earlier stated concerning the incident in Hrasnica that Serbs were attacking for three days in a row, is that correct, that part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of Sarajevo was under pressure at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, were you aware of the fact that Hrasnica was, in fact, a very important location where soldiers of the ABiH were present?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that it was certainly a front line location; and if it was a front line location, then ABiH soldier would have been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So there was a time of intense fighting. Is that the right way to put it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a time when the intensity of the fighting was increasing, and we were aware that this kind of a showdown was about to occur, yes. I could just add that I'm not responsible for the selection of the videos. I am only a witness, but I think the report was reasonably fair and balanced because it showed what was happening in two areas, and people can draw whatever conclusions they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the break now. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, we're now going to carry on. We've looked at the video from start to end of April 7th, 1995, and in your comments --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: We heard your comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as a witness at the time, can you confirm to us that before April, there had been a lull on the Sarajevo front line?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been, to my recollection, a relative lull. There had been quite a lot going on in other front lines around the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, specifically, in the Sarajevo area as a whole, it's fair to say that in early 1995 and up to the beginning of the spring, this was a relatively quiet time and the cease-fire was in fact respected.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to look at document together. I don't think that you have seen this document before, but it's a part of our case file. It's Exhibit D163, and I'd like to stress at this point we were take being April 7th, 1995. You, in your report, were stating that for three days the Serbs had been attacking Hrasnica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you tell me the words that were used, they certainly attacked it on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I'm trying to quote you what you're saying in the clip that we just watched, in the video. You were saying, and maybe we could watch it again. You were saying that the Serbs had been in the offensive for three days in a row at Hrasnica, which is a suburb of Sarajevo. I think that is roughly what you were say?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that, I said that. I'm certainly not going to waste your time by asking to you play it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Quite. Now, what I'd like you to do now is to look at this exhibit -- Defence exhibit that you can see here is a letter written by Mr. Rasim Delic. Is that a name that rings a bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. He was the commander of the ABiH at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And he writes to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who was the president at the time of Bosnia. I'd like to you look at the document and particularly the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: It says here, I'm going to read it in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: To the counsel, please read the portion in B/C/S again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're being asked to read the B/C/S portion again, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was merely trying to draw your attention. We can read it in English here as well: "[In English] We will defend ourselves." [Interpretation] Do you read that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes I see it. What particular part do you wish to draw my attention, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's around the middle starting, "[In English] We will defend ourselves."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We must continue saying that we will defend ourselves." Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, upon reading this, does it look to you that Mr. Rasim Delic is displeased with the cease-fire, that he is not happy with it. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the fair to say that he is planning an offensive. He is planning to break the siege, and I think that was consistent with the second part of my report. That is what the soldiers were training for inside. So this doesn't surprise me at all, nor does it surprise me that he says that "we will defending ourselves" when in fact they were attacking. That is, in fact, what they did. What everybody did. I see no surprise in this. I just wish I had access to it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And since the document is already an exhibit, I'd like to have the whole of the clip of the video that we've seen tendered. Parts of that is already exhibit P 261, but I would like to have the Defence exhibit be the whole of this video, meaning video number 65 ter V000-7060, minute 30, 40 seconds, to the 11th minute, 53rd second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, would you just explain to us again your understanding of the sentence, "We must continue saying that we will defend ourselves and that we will not be the first to attack."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on both sides of this war, certainly at that time, they would always say they were responding to attacks, rather than initiating attacks. It was also a time when we in the Sarajevo press corps were aware that there was an offensive coming up, we had heard reports of the BiH fighters being moved from Central Bosnia closer to Sarajevo and even through the tunnel in Sarajevo. To prepare for it, there was one special forces unit called the Black Swans, who were involved in these military movements of soldiers, troop movements. What I'm saying, Your Honour, is I don't see anything that surprises me in that interesting paragraph, but it really confirms the kinds of things that we were saying at the time, in the sense that an offensive was imminent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, starting from this time - I'm referring to the time when fighting started again in April - do you recall if that was the beginning of a time of rather intensive fighting and that was going to carry on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say that the fighting in April was so intensive, except in the capture of Mount Vlasic, which I have in my notes of the 9th of April. I was not here for the rest of April so I can't answer that; but certainly in May, it became very intense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And after June 1995, were you also --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, I'm waiting. The Chamber is conferring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If you would care to look at what you were doing in June 1995, were you in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And in that month of June, did you notice how intense fighting was? I'm referring specifically to the area -- the urban area, really along the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would specific it was particularly heavy on the 7th and the 8th of June, according to my records.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And further on, if you still have your notes, were you still in Sarajevo on June 15th and 16th?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My notes tell me there was a BiH offensive on the 15th and an attempted break out of the city on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now to complement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To conclude the examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at 65 ter number DD00-7060.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We already watched part of this video yesterday. It's a BBC dated April 9th, 1995. I would have liked to watch it together, the whole thing. So we can have all of the information it contains as it was given to the television viewers by yourself. This was Exhibit 616 and we are now going to see the video as a whole. That is the 35th minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, there, Mr. Bell, we've seen a fragment that we didn't see yesterday of this news report concerning these soldiers, a liaison officers, Serb liaison officers, that had been expelled, to go by what they are saying, by General Smith. I presume that refers to General Rupert Smith, who was at the time commander in that sector of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you be in a position to explain what you're showing in this news report, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can say by the branding on the top of the screen that we couldn't get to Pale at the time so we took it off air. These were two liaison officers who been based in the Gornji Vakuf at the UN base there, as part of a confidence building measure, I think, put in at about the time of the Christmas cease-fire. It was -- there was a lot of unhappiness inside UNPROFOR about this decision to expel these two liaison officers and the way it was -- it was handled. That's all I can tell from memory, but I had good friends inside the UNPROFOR headquarters. I know there was some fierce debates at which it was concluded that was not well handled. This whole matter was not well handled by UNPROFOR. As for the video in general, if the UN told me they were expecting a Serb offensive, then they were expecting a Serb offensive. But I think as I tried to explain as even-handedly as I did, there was fighting on both sides, and it was pretty clear to us that a military showdown was imminent. But the expulsion of these two -- these two liaison officers, I suppose, was another sign of how bad it was getting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry about that. I would like to have this part of video, 65 ter number V000-7160, tendered as evidence, 35th minute to 36, 26 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just to check with the registrar, was the earlier video duly tendered and given a number? I'm speaking of the one dated April 7th.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't have the dates. However, I have DD00-7160 tendered and admitted as D181.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I also want to thank Mr. Bell. It was a great honour to me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, actually just one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, today at page 7 of the transcript line 25, you were asked whether you recalled saying yesterday that the situation regarding food in Sarajevo had improved in the spring of 1995; and without the transcript in front of you, you said: "I probably said that." Now, Mr. Bell, you have the transcript in front of you, and I'd like to direct you to page 60, line 20. And for the record, I can read what appears on the page in front of you. When asked whether these privations endured throughout the war, you said: "Like the fighting, they fluctuated. There were periods during winter lulls, during cease-fires, during temporary agreements where gas and electricity were intermittently restored. There was a period when the food situation got better; but come April 1995, the plight of the civilians inside Sarajevo was as desperate as it had been at any time." Do you stand by what you said yesterday, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No other questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for come together Tribunal to give it and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President. The next witness will be W-156, who will be in closed session, pursuant to your decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the name of the witness, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ijaz Hussain Malik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: I think if is the witness is not protected, one, you should remove the curtain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you start by stating your full name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: I'm Ijaz Hussain Malik, and my date of birth is 20th of the October, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, can I lead the witness through personal details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Malik, are you, presently, a colonel in the Pakistan army?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you joined the Pakistan army in 1979; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Yes, October 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your remit or speciality is infantry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm in infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you deployed for Dessert Storm in 1990 with the Pakistani army?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Yes, i was part of Pakistani contingent, and it wasn't in the main sector. It was on one the sides towards Yemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, were you deployed with the United Nations, firstly, in Zagreb in October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Say it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you deployed with the United Nations in Zagreb in October 1994, as part of the Pakistani contingent?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: It wasn't part of the Pakistani contingent. At the start of my mission as military observer, I was initially posted in Zagreb as air field monitor, and there after the second mission was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: As an air field monitor what were your primary duties?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: As an air field monitor, I had three duties. Number one was there was an office right inside the airport, and we had to man that office. Number two was there was a radar, again, in the airport. It was part of that civil airport. One panel was given to us, and we had to monitor that and report the violations. And the third one was it was patrolling of the area. There were two Croatia air bases. One was pretty close to the airport and the another was a little further away about ten, 12 kilometres away. We had to go there and just [indiscernible] the aircrafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said in an earlier answer that you were then deployed to Sarajevo. When was that?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: When I was deployed there, is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: The first six months, I think from 14th October to probably 30th of April, I was in Zagreb; and, thereafter, from first of May till end of mission, which was 14th of October, 1995, I was on the strength of the Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where were you deployed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Initially, I was deployed in a team. Sierra India was probably the name, and the place was Hrasnica. It was on the outskirts of the Sarajevo. It is a little away from Sarajevo city main.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say your team, do you mean UN Military Observer team?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Yeah. We used to stay as a team. There used to be ten, 12 military observers from different countries living together in a civil hired accommodation. So, initially, yes, it was Hrasnica. We were about ten, and we were in Hrasnica for about two months. Later on, the position was changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that you were about ten people in the team. Do you recall who was your team leader?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: When I went there, I think, for first one or two weeks, probably it was a British officer. I don't remember his name, but he was a captain, as far as the rank is concerned. And after about one or two weeks, it was changed. He left the mission and somebody else, I think it was Captain Melum from Norway. He was a Norwegian officer. He was the one who took over as team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you were posted to Zagreb, and before you arrived in Sarajevo in May 1995, did you undergo any training; and if so, what kind of training did you have?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: As such, there was no formal training meant for me. Any UNMO, when they were going in the mission, they were given, initially, a few tests, tests for the UN entry. And, thereafter, it was about three days, I think, general training. That included how to fill in certain forms and going right to different places, in case you're posted to a hard area, like, Sarajevo where it is more active. So a very cursory sort of, what do you call it, training. In general, you can't call a course; but, certainly, three days for filling out the forms and knowing the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in those three days, did you undergo training with respect to investigations that -- that you would do once you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
utterances.text: Yeah. To some extent - I would not say 100 per cent - I was introduced with certain formats, and those were basic things. I mean, there was nothing to be trained in that. We were just trained for three days, four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your career with the Pakistani army, have you had training in what is termed as crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK
